gap: No result ChatGPT got states a temperature measured by a named reviewer on any candidate adapter: EVadept's Mike Becker measured the TeslaTap Mini at 102°F at its hottest point after an hour of charging. The current used and the measuring method were not published, and no lab has published temperature data for the Lectron 80A UL 2252 or the A2Z Stellar.
standout_why: Pages compared: Plug & Range's Lectron 48A review (updated 2026-08-20), which says it has not bench-tested; EV & Charger's best-adapters guide (2026-10-05), which only claims 80 A adapters 'run noticeably cooler' with no data; The Charge Curve's Lectron vs A2Z (updated 2026-10-17), which says 'We do not run a testing lab'; and the TeslaTap maker page, which has no test data. The Lectron 'Tested' blog post at rank 8 is in ChatGPT's results but uncited. It reposts Forbes Home's test, which has charging figures but no temperatures. So the one charging measurement on these pages is already in ChatGPT's results. thisWATT's guide and product page are the cited rivals, and I could not open them: both fail with a self-signed certificate error, so I could not check them. The EVadept temperatures are new compared with the pages I could read. But they are from 2023, use an unstated method, and come from a page that confuses product names. That is too weak to be the fact this page stands on.
decides: This confirms the pick and does not change it. No named lab measured the two UL 2252 picks (Lectron 80A, A2Z Stellar) under sustained load, so measurements cannot rank them. The case for them still rests on the UL 2252 listing and temperature sensors their makers state. The only published heat figure for the TeslaTap Mini (EVadept, 102°F after an hour) does not mark it as unsafe or as better. The page should not claim one adapter 'runs cooler' as a measured fact.

findings.label: Hottest-point temperature after 1 hour of charging
findings.source_title: 5 Best Tesla to J1772 Adapters that easily charge non-Tesla EVs • Expert Guide (EVadept)
findings.note: By Mike Becker, reviewed by David Perez, updated 2023-10-02. Quote: 'when charging at the maximum allowable voltage for an hour, the device showed a temperature of 102°F at the hottest point.' The test current and the TeslaTap Mini variant (40/60/80 A) are not stated. The measuring method (thermometer or thermal camera) is not stated.

findings.label: Peak temperature, 60 min at 40 A / 9.6 kW
findings.value: did not exceed 99 (unit not stated, presumably °F)
findings.source_title: 5 Best Tesla to J1772 Adapters that easily charge non-Tesla EVs • Expert Guide (EVadept)
findings.note: Same author and date as above. The page calls this unit 'Lectron mini', and its spec table lists it at 48 A, but the test ran at 40 A. That leaves it unclear whether this is the 48A model. The page says it excluded products that heated above 105°F.

findings.label: Charging delivered on a Tesla destination charger (2023 Hyundai Ioniq 5 Limited)
findings.value: 'full 48 amp charge at an average 9.6 kWh' (as published)
findings.source_title: Tested: Lectron 48 Amp Tesla Charging Adapter (Lectron EV blog, repost of Forbes Home review)
findings.note: Byline Joel Manansala. Original Forbes Home post dated 2023-07-28, reposted 2024-09-15 on Lectron's site; I could not find the original on forbes.com. Lectron loaned the unit. The test used two older hotel destination chargers. The figures don't add up: 48 A × 240 V ≈ 11.5 kW, while 9.6 kW ≈ 40 A. A 2018 Nissan Leaf SV in the same test was limited by its 6.6 kW / 30 A onboard charger. No temperatures were recorded and there was no long-term test. This page is in ChatGPT's results at rank 8, uncited.

findings.label: Owner field report: connector temperature and thermal shutdown (one defective unit)
findings.value: 117°F connector reading; dropped from 11.7 kW and shut off after 3–5 min; replacement unit 'works perfectly'
findings.source_title: A2Z NACS to J1772 overheating (F150 Lightning Forum)
findings.note: Forum owner 'flyct' (Jerry), not a reviewer or lab, posts dated 2024-11-11 to 11-14. The reading came from the Wall Monitor for Tesla app polling a Tesla Gen 3 Wall Connector. A2Z replaced the unit and the poster concluded the first one was defective. For comparison, an off-brand 48 A adapter held 11.7 kW for 10+ min with a 125.5°F peak in direct sun, and an off-brand 80 A adapter held it with a 132.6°F peak. This is one owner's anecdote; use it as context only.

findings.label: Maker-published test data
findings.value: none published; maker states 60 A continuous @ 250 VAC (15 kW), $194.96
findings.note: No temperature-rise figure, certification or warranty is stated on the page.

findings.label: Hands-on use, Chevy Bolt EUV at a hotel Tesla destination charger
findings.value: no measured amps, kW or temperature reported
findings.note: Jennifer Sensiba, 2022-12-11. She charged 'a few hours until full'. Listed so the page doesn't count it as a measurement.

I searched for RTINGS-, Car and Driver-, InsideEVs-, Electrek- and Out of Spec-style tests and found none. I tried to open Lectron's 80A product page for its SGS data; it returned HTTP 429.

Measured temperature or delivered kW for the A2Z Stellar from a named reviewer. EV America credits State of Charge (Tom Moloughney) with endorsing it, but I could not find the video or any figures from it. The A2Z product page returned HTTP 429 twice.
Any measurement for the TeslaTap Mini 60A or 80A at a stated test current.
The thisWATT guide and TeslaTap spec page (both cited by ChatGPT): fetch failed with a self-signed certificate error, so I could not check whether they contain measurements.
The original Forbes Home article on forbes.com, to confirm the 9.6 kW / 48 A wording and the author; I only found Lectron's repost.
